name: 旬の天ぷらと季節料理 吉福 (Shun no Tenpura to Kisetsu Ryori Kichifuku)

claims.text: Tempura is fried in shared fryers using wheat-flour batter as the core technique. Cross-contamination of any non-battered item with wheat flour is near-certain in a tempura kitchen. No source mentions any GF-safe fryer or protocol.

Himeji oden is served with ginger soy sauce. Tempura dipping sauce (tentsuyu) typically contains soy sauce and mirin. Standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat. No tamari or GF soy sauce alternative is mentioned anywhere.

The menu is built around seafood and dashi-based broths. Tempura batter likely contains egg. Miso soup accompaniments and chawanmushi (savory egg custard with shrimp) are standard menu items. No vegan-safe prep path is identifiable.

name: 蕎麦切り 谷口 (Sobakiri Taniguchi)

claims.text: The kitchen is a shared, compact space (~33 m²) serving wheat-containing soba and tempura; no dedicated GF zone or fryer is mentioned anywhere.
Standard soy-based tsuyu is used for soba dipping broth. One review notes 'salt and wasabi' as an optional seasoning (塩と山葵で), but ordinary wheat-containing soy sauce is implied as the default.
Freshly made dashi (作りたてのお出汁) is cited by a reviewer — in this traditional context almost certainly bonito (鰹節) based. No plant-based dashi alternative is mentioned.

No information on dedicated fryer or separate preparation surfaces. Papad (Indian lentil cracker) is served as a topping — traditional papad is naturally gluten-free, but shared kitchen risk is unknown.
Hinepon (chicken ponzu) and pickled accompaniments may contain soy sauce with wheat. No explicit wheat-free soy sauce or tamari use is stated anywhere.
The vegan bean curry is served alongside chicken and shrimp curries in a shared kitchen. No statement about separate utensils or prep surfaces for the vegan option.
No allergy handling policy or staff training is documented. The shop is a tiny owner-run counter with 11 seats — direct communication with the owner-chef is the realistic path for dietary questions.

The tofu and bean curry was explicitly created without any animal products for vegan and allergy-aware tourists — demonstrating owner awareness of dietary needs, unusual for a small Japanese curry counter.
Spice-based curries (rather than Japanese roux blocks) avoid the wheat-laden roux found in most Japanese curry restaurants, reducing one common gluten source.
Shared charcoal grill used for both seafood and chicken; no separation for allergen-sensitive diners mentioned anywhere.
Soy sauce (wheat-containing) is a fundamental ingredient in izakaya cooking — tare for yakitori, marinades, and dipping sauces all apply here. No tamari or wheat-free soy sauce options are indicated.
All menu items involve seafood or chicken; no vegan dishes exist to evaluate for cross-contact.
No allergy-handling policy or allergen menu is noted on any platform reviewed. Inquiries would need to be made in Japanese directly with staff.
Plain sashimi (without soy sauce) is the single category most likely to be free of added wheat — the kitchen does receive and serve raw seafood that has not been marinated.

name: 炭焼あなご やま義 (Sumiyaki Anago Yamayoshi)

claims.text: 14-seat open kitchen with no separation between preparation areas; no information about dedicated fryers or wheat-free cooking zones.

House tare — applied repeatedly to eel during charcoal grilling — is made with standard Japanese soy sauce, which contains wheat. Dashi soup served alongside also likely uses wheat-containing soy sauce. No tamari or wheat-free soy sauce alternative mentioned.
All dishes are fish/eel-based; the kitchen has no plant-based cooking track and vegan cross-contact is unavoidable.
No allergy handling information is published. Given the tiny size (14 seats) and single-specialty format, detailed allergy inquiries would need to be made by phone in Japanese before visiting.
Single-ingredient specialty kitchen (conger eel only) means no cross-contact from unrelated proteins or cuisines found in multi-concept restaurants.

No information on cross-contamination protocols has been published. The kitchen handles wheat-based shoyu, tare, and potentially tempura batter — standard risk for a traditional sushi-kaiseki kitchen.

Standard Japanese shoyu (wheat-containing) is used for nigiri and dipping; the house-made nitsume (anago glaze) is soy-sauce based and therefore also contains wheat. No tamari or GF shoyu option is advertised.
Fish-based dashi underpins the kaiseki cooking. Conger eel, sea bream, octopus, and other marine proteins are handled throughout the kitchen with no plant-only preparation zone documented.

The restaurant states it aims for 'safe and reliable meals' for all ages and uses domestic traceable ingredients, but publishes no formal allergen matrix or allergy protocol. Same-day phone reservations are accepted, making it possible to communicate needs in advance.

Exclusive use of wild-caught Seto Inland Sea conger eel (no farmed or imported substitutes) and rice from the owner's own paddies — traceability of key ingredients is unusually strong for a restaurant of this type.

name: 大衆酒場 蒼 (Taishū Sakaba Sou)

claims.text: No information about cross-contamination controls is available. This is a 12-seat counter izakaya with a compact kitchen; dedicated fryer or allergen segregation is not documented.
Standard soy sauce containing wheat is used throughout Japanese izakaya cuisine. No tamari or gluten-free soy sauce alternatives are mentioned anywhere in available sources.
Typical izakaya kitchen where fish-based dashi (katsuobushi/bonito) is standard in sauces, soups, and cooking bases. No vegan preparation protocols documented.
No allergy-handling policy or English-language accommodation is documented. Reservations are made via Instagram DM in Japanese; allergen queries would need to be raised there in advance.
Small, owner-operated venue where direct communication with the proprietor is possible, making advance allergy enquiries via Instagram DM (@sou.taishusakaba) feasible before visiting.

name: 大衆酒場 フレンチマン 姫路店 (Taishuu Sakaba Frenchman Himeji)

claims.text: パスタ（リングイネ）、ホットサンド（朝メニュー）など小麦を含む料理が多数あり、調理場での交差汚染リスクが高いと推定される。公式情報なし。
フレンチベースのため醤油使用は限定的と思われるが、和風アレンジ料理（串焼き等）でのたれ・醤油使用の有無は未確認。
フォアグラ・バター・生クリームなど動物性食材がメニューの中核を担っており、ヴィーガン対応の区別は困難と推定。公式のアレルギー対応情報なし。
アレルギー対応に関する公式情報・スタッフ訓練の案内は取材記事・公式サイト・食べログのいずれにも記載がない。来店前に電話（079-280-4555）での確認を推奨。
野菜を活かした小皿料理が複数あり、野菜中心の食事を好む方には選択肢が存在する。
